The space station orbited a desolate planet, its metallic corridors echoing with the solitary hum of machinery. Outside the viewing ports, a ballet of asteroids danced against the inky backdrop of space. This station, known as Outpost Theta-9, was established during the Great Expansion Era, a time when humanity sought to mine the rare isotopes found in the debris fields of the shattered moon of Kaelos. The planet below, once a lush world teeming with prehistoric flora, was stripped bare by centuries of aggressive terraforming and resource extraction, leaving behind a gray, cratered husk that reflected the cold light of a distant sun. The station's crew, a small team of engineers and geologists, lived in a state of perpetual isolation, their lives dictated by the rhythmic cycles of the station's life support systems and the constant, low-frequency vibration of the mining drills below. The asteroids outside were not merely rocks but remnants of a catastrophic collision that had occurred millennia ago, their orbits stabilized by the gravitational pull of the dead planet, creating a mesmerizing yet dangerous dance that served as both a backdrop and a threat to the fragile human presence in the void.
